questions.question: The passage primarily argues that:
questions.solution: The passage says repair 'has been priced out' (para 1), explains this through rising relative costs (para 2), and concludes that making repair cheaper beats making people feel guilty (paras 3–5). Option 1 is the view the author rejects ('not … consumer laziness'). Option 3 is described as how the rules are 'often described', and the author says their deeper effect is economic. Option 4 is never claimed: technicians work at the same speed, not with less skill.
options: consumers today repair less than earlier generations because they value their possessions less
the decline of repair is driven mainly by shifting relative prices, so policy should narrow the cost gap rather than appeal to values
right-to-repair rules are essentially consumer-protection measures
manufacturing efficiency has made repair technicians less skilled over time

questions.question: According to the passage, why has repair become relatively more expensive?
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: in low-productivity sectors 'wages must still keep pace with the rest of the economy, so prices rise', while manufacturing prices fall. A technician 'works at roughly the same speed … yet must be paid a modern wage'. There is no comparison of technicians' wages with factory wages (option 1). Supply chains are linked to cheap manufacturing, not missing parts (option 3). Consumer taste for features (option 4) is never mentioned.
options: Repair technicians now demand higher wages than factory workers
Repair productivity has barely changed, while wages must keep pace with an economy in which manufactured goods keep getting cheaper
Long supply chains have made spare parts impossible to obtain
Consumers increasingly prefer new models with more features

questions.question: With which of the following would the author most likely agree?
questions.solution: The author says 'moral appeals will achieve little' and lists lower taxes on repair among the 'more promising interventions' that 'target the price gap directly'. Option 1 contradicts this. Option 3 contradicts 'None of this means that culture is irrelevant'. Option 4 contradicts the claim that people sensibly 'respond to the costs in front of them'.
options: A public campaign urging people to cherish their belongings would substantially raise repair rates
A tax cut on repair services is likely to do more to increase repair than an awareness campaign
Cultural habits have no influence on whether people choose to repair
Households that replace broken appliances instead of repairing them are acting irrationally

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
questions.solution: The argument rests on prices being the main driver of repair decisions. If repair becoming cheaper changed nothing, that link is undercut. Options 2 and 3 are consistent with, and even support, the cost-disease explanation. Option 4 says nothing about whether prices drive behaviour.
options: In a region where subsidies made repair clearly cheaper than replacement, repair rates did not rise at all
Repair technicians' real wages have risen over the past fifty years
New appliances have become cheaper in real terms
Some manufacturers have lobbied against right-to-repair rules

questions.question: The example of the two drivers is used mainly to:
questions.solution: The paragraph ends: 'The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled', and the next paragraph names this 'moral luck'. The passage says nothing about the penalties being lenient (option 1). It never says the second driver is blameless (option 3). Option 4 is one view discussed later (the 'inner will' view), not the purpose of the example.
options: show that drink-driving penalties are too lenient
illustrate a case in which our judgements of blame seem to depend on something outside the agents' control
argue that the second driver deserves no blame at all
demonstrate that intentions matter more than outcomes

questions.question: According to the passage, the main difficulty with applying the control principle consistently is that it:
questions.solution: Paragraph 3: the principle 'threatens to swallow almost everything' (temperament, upbringing, circumstances), and 'it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged'. Option 3 is the reverse: the principle focuses on what we control, including intentions. Options 1 and 4 concern the law, which isn't the stated difficulty.
options: would make the law too harsh on careless drivers
would leave little or nothing open to moral judgement, since so much that shapes us is beyond our control
cannot account for the intentions of agents
conflicts with the way courts assign penalties

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that only the 'inner will' should be judged is best described as:
questions.solution: 'This view has the merit of consistency, but it struggles to explain experiences that seem central to moral life.' The author grants a strength (so not contempt), raises a serious objection (so not endorsement), and clearly evaluates it (so not neutral).
options: acknowledging its consistency while doubting that it fits our moral experience

questions.question: Which of the following can best be inferred about the author's own position?
questions.solution: The final paragraph presents acceptance sympathetically and ends by suggesting that 'the demand that morality be perfectly fair was itself a fantasy', which signals agreement. Option 1 is the view the author resists. Option 3 has no support. Option 4 contradicts 'The second driver will rightly feel something'.
options: The author thinks moral luck should be eliminated from our moral practices
The author leans towards accepting moral luck, even if this makes morality less tidy and less fair
The author believes the first driver is more blameworthy than the second
The author regards the second driver's regret as irrational

questions.question: According to the passage, the replication crisis is mainly explained by:
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: 'deliberate fabrication explains only a small part', and 'the deeper causes are structural': journals preferring striking results, plus 'many small decisions' that can 'make chance patterns look like real discoveries'. Options 3 and 4 are never mentioned.
options: publication incentives and many small analytical choices that can make chance patterns look like real findings
journals refusing to publish psychology research

questions.question: Which of the following statements about statistical significance is consistent with the passage?
questions.solution: Paragraph 3 says this almost word for word. Option 1 is the misreading the passage warns against. Option 3 contradicts 'The statistical threshold itself has come in for criticism' and the role of nudging results 'across the conventional threshold'. Option 4 is the reverse of the final sentence of paragraph 3.
options: A significant result means there is at most a five per cent chance that the finding is false
Whether a significant result reflects a real effect depends partly on the hypothesis's prior plausibility and the study's statistical power
Significance thresholds played no role in the replication crisis
Testing many hypotheses in small samples makes false alarms rarer

questions.question: As described in the passage, the main purpose of a registered report is to:
questions.solution: The journal agrees to publish 'on the strength of its design, before the results are known, removing the incentive to produce a striking outcome'. Speed (option 1) isn't mentioned. Option 3 is what preregistration prevents. Option 4 is never stated.
options: speed up the publication of results
make the decision to publish independent of whether the results turn out to be striking
allow researchers to revise their analysis after seeing the data
replace peer review with public registration

questions.question: The reformers' reply in the final paragraph implies that:
questions.solution: 'The aim is not to forbid researchers from following hunches, but to stop hunches confirmed after the fact from being presented as predictions made in advance.' Option 1 contradicts 'exploration is welcome'. Option 3 contradicts the critics' point that exploration 'often precedes genuine breakthroughs', which the reformers don't dispute. Option 4 isn't stated.
options: the problem is not exploration itself but presenting after-the-fact findings as if they had been predicted
hunches rarely lead to genuine breakthroughs
critics have misunderstood the statistics behind preregistration

questions.question: The author's central claim is that:
questions.solution: The final paragraph states the author's conclusion: 'A translation is better understood as a reading', and many translations are 'evidence of the poem's richness'. Option 1 is called 'an exaggeration'. Option 2 ignores the failures of strict fidelity the author describes. Option 4 is only one method mentioned in paragraph 4, never a universal rule.
options: poetry cannot be translated in any meaningful sense
literal translations are always preferable to free ones
a translation is best seen as one partial reading rather than a replacement, so many translations reflect a poem's richness rather than failure
translators should always add explanatory notes

questions.question: The 'pressed flower' comparison suggests that strictly faithful translations can:
questions.solution: Such translations are 'accurate in every particular and lifeless as a whole', like a flower keeping 'the shape of a bloom but none of its scent'. Option 1 contradicts 'accurate in every particular'. Options 3 and 4 have no support.
options: keep a poem's form and particulars while losing its living effect
become more beautiful than the original
be impossible for ordinary readers to understand

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about translations admired 'as poems in their own right'?
questions.solution: Such admiration is 'both a tribute to the translator and a quiet admission of distance from the source'. Option 1 is the opposite. Option 3 contradicts 'celebrated'. Option 4 describes the third approach, which is a different method.
options: They prove that the translator stayed closest to the original
Their being admired in this way hints that they may have moved away from the source poem
They are rarely successful with readers
They usually print the original and a literal version side by side

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely consider an honest way of dealing with what is lost in translation?
questions.solution: Paragraph 4 says these methods 'treat the loss honestly rather than disguising it'. Options 1 and 4 disguise changes. Option 3 avoids the problem rather than dealing with it, and the passage never suggests it.
options: Presenting a free recreation without mentioning the original's wordplay
Publishing the original with a literal and a freer version, along with notes on puns and allusions
Translating only poems that contain no wordplay
Updating the poem's imagery for modern readers without comment

Its advantages are real: saved commuting time, wider hiring pools and greater flexibility for carers. But organisations have discovered costs that are harder to measure. When parents conclude that their children's prospects depend on a dominant language, they speak it at home, and within a generation or two the older tongue survives mainly among the elderly. Efforts at revival therefore succeed less through nostalgia than through making the language useful again, in schools, media, local government and work.

Elderly speakers bear the main responsibility for keeping languages alive.
Nostalgia is the strongest force behind successful language revival.

A well-designed default can shape behaviour as powerfully as a rule. When employees are automatically enrolled in a pension scheme and must opt out, participation is far higher than when they must actively opt in, even though the choice on offer is identical. Defaults work because people tend to stay with whatever requires no action. That gives the designers of forms and systems a quiet but considerable power, and with it a responsibility to set defaults in people's interest.
questions.solution: The paragraph moves from evidence (auto-enrolment) to mechanism (inertia) to conclusion (power and responsibility). Option 2 has all three. Option 1 isn't argued. Option 3 overstates 'as powerfully as'. Option 4 is never stated: the point is inertia, not indifference.
options: Pension schemes should be made compulsory for all employees.
Because people tend to stick with defaults, those who set them hold real influence and should use it in people's interest.
Defaults are more effective than laws in every situation.
Most employees are indifferent to their pensions.

Critics have stopped museums from returning objects to their places of origin.

Yet research on learning suggests that memories formed during the day are strengthened and reorganised during sleep, and that people deprived of it perform worse on tasks requiring both recall and judgement. Cutting sleep to gain working hours may therefore lower the quality of the very work it is meant to increase.
questions.solution: The paragraph's conclusion ('therefore…') is that cutting sleep can backfire on work quality because sleep supports memory and judgement. That is option 2. Option 1 gives a specific figure that isn't in the text. Options 3 and 4 are unrelated claims.
options: Everyone should sleep for more than eight hours a night.
Because sleep supports memory and judgement, giving it up for extra working time can undermine the work itself.
Productivity is impossible to measure accurately.

questions.question: With 20 coins, how many coins must Asha remove on her first turn to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. 20 − 2 = 18 is a multiple of 3. Taking 1 (19) or 4 (16) leaves a winning pile for Bilal.

questions.question: Suppose players may remove 1, 2, 3 or 4 coins (last coin still wins). With 23 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?

questions.question: Now suppose the rule is reversed: the player who takes the last coin LOSES (moves are still 1, 2 or 4). With 10 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Now a pile of 1 is losing for the player to move, because they must take the last coin. Working upward: 2, 3 → can leave 1, so winning. 4 → leaves 3, 2 or 0, and 0 means you just took the last coin and lost, so 4 is losing. questions.question: A trader marks his goods 50% above cost price and then allows two successive discounts of 10% and 20%. What is his profit percentage?
questions.solution: SP = CP × 1.5 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 1.08 × CP, so the profit is 8%.

questions.question: Ravi's income rises by 20% and his expenditure rises by 10%. As a result, his savings rise by 50%. What percentage of his original income did he originally save?
questions.solution: Let income = 100 and expenditure = E. New savings: 120 − 1.1E = 1.5(100 − E) ⇒ 0.4E = 30 ⇒ E = 75. Savings = 25% of income.

questions.question: A shopkeeper sells an article at a 20% profit. Had he bought it for 10% less and sold it for ₹18 less, his profit would have been 25%. What is the cost price (in ₹)?

In a two-candidate election, 10% of registered voters did not vote and 10% of the votes cast were invalid. The winner got 54% of the valid votes and won by 1,620 votes. How many registered voters were there?
questions.solution: Valid votes = 0.9 × 0.9 × N = 0.81N. The margin is 54% − 46% = 8% of valid votes: 0.08 × 0.81N = 0.0648N = 1620 ⇒ N = 25,000.

questions.question: Two cars start at the same time from P and Q and drive towards each other. After they meet, the car from P takes 4 hours to reach Q and the car from Q takes 9 hours to reach P. If the car from P travels at 45 km/h, what is the distance PQ (in km)?
questions.solution: If the meeting happens after t hours: t² = 4 × 9 ⇒ t = 6 h, and speed ratio = √(9/4) = 3 : 2, so the other car does 30 km/h. PQ = (45 + 30) × 6 = 450 km. Check: P-car covers 270 km before meeting, then the remaining 180 km at 45 km/h = 4 h ✓.

questions.question: A train passes a man walking at 3 km/h in the same direction in 10 seconds, and a man walking at 6 km/h towards it in 8 seconds. What is the length of the train?

A and B start together from the same point on a 1,200 m circular track and run in the same direction at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. After how many seconds will they first be together at the starting point again?
questions.solution: A completes a lap every 240 s and B every 1200/7 s. Both are at the start at times that are multiples of both: 240a = 1200b/7 ⇒ 7a = 5b, smallest a = 5 ⇒ 1,200 s. (They do meet at 600 s too, but halfway round the track, not at the start.)

questions.question: A boat goes 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours. It goes 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours. What is the speed of the stream?
questions.solution: Let u = 1/upstream speed and d = 1/downstream speed: 30u + 44d = 10 and 40u + 55d = 13. Solving gives u = 1/5 and d = 1/11, so the upstream speed is 5 and the downstream speed 11. Stream = (11 − 5)/2 = 3 km/h.

questions.question: Walking at 5 km/h, Meera reaches office 6 minutes late. Walking at 6 km/h, she reaches 4 minutes early. How far is her office?
questions.solution: The time difference is 10 min = 1/6 h. d/5 − d/6 = 1/6 ⇒ d/30 = 1/6 ⇒ d = 5 km.

questions.question: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days, B and C in 15 days, and C and A in 20 days. In how many days can A alone finish it?
12 men or 18 women can finish a piece of work in 14 days. How many days will 8 men and 16 women take to finish it?
questions.solution: 1 man = 18/12 = 1.5 women. 8 men + 16 women = 28 women. Work = 18 × 14 = 252 woman-days ⇒ 252/28 = 9 days.

questions.question: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 20 and 30 minutes respectively, and pipe C empties it in 15 minutes. All three are opened on an empty tank, and C is closed after 10 minutes. How many minutes in total does it take to fill the tank?
questions.solution: With all three open: 1/20 + 1/30 − 1/15 = 1/60 per minute, so 10 minutes fill 1/6. The remaining 5/6 at A + B = 1/12 per minute takes 10 minutes. Total = 20 minutes.

questions.question: A is twice as efficient as B, and together they finish a job in 14 days. How many days would A alone take?
questions.solution: If B does b per day, A does 2b, so 3b = 1/14 ⇒ b = 1/42 and A = 1/21 ⇒ 21 days.

questions.question: A 60-litre mixture of milk and water contains 20% water. How many litres of water must be added so that water becomes 25% of the new mixture?
questions.solution: Milk = 48 L and stays fixed. For 75% milk, total = 48/0.75 = 64 L, so add 4 L of water.

questions.question: A vessel contains 80 litres of pure wine. 8 litres are taken out and replaced with water, and this is done three times in all. How much wine is left?
questions.solution: Each operation keeps 72/80 = 0.9 of the wine. Wine left = 80 × 0.9³ = 58.32 L.

questions.question: Alloy X has copper and zinc in the ratio 3 : 2, and alloy Y has them in the ratio 1 : 3. In what ratio (X : Y) must they be mixed to get an alloy with equal amounts of copper and zinc?
questions.solution: Copper fraction: X = 0.6, Y = 0.25, target 0.5. By alligation, X : Y = (0.5 − 0.25) : (0.6 − 0.5) = 0.25 : 0.1 = 5 : 2.

Riya deposits ₹1,000 at the start of each year for 2 years in an account paying 10% per annum compounded annually. What is the balance (in ₹) at the end of the second year?
questions.solution: The first deposit grows for 2 years: 1000 × 1.21 = 1210. The second grows for 1 year: 1000 × 1.1 = 1100. Total = ₹2,310.

questions.question: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. Six years ago they were in the ratio 2 : 3. What is the sum of their present ages?
questions.solution: (5k − 6)/(7k − 6) = 2/3 ⇒ 15k − 18 = 14k − 12 ⇒ k = 6. The ages are 30 and 42, so the sum is 72.

questions.question: A bag has ₹1, 50-paise and 25-paise coins in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 by number, worth ₹216 in total. How many 50-paise coins are there?
questions.solution: Value per set of (2, 3, 4) coins = 2 + 1.5 + 1 = ₹4.5. Sets = 216/4.5 = 48. 50-paise coins = 3 × 48 = 144.

The roots of x² − px + 12 = 0 differ by 1, and p > 0. What is p?
questions.solution: (r₁ − r₂)² = (r₁ + r₂)² − 4r₁r₂ = p² − 48 = 1 ⇒ p = 7. (The roots are 3 and 4.)

questions.question: For how many integer values of k does x² + kx + 16 = 0 have no real roots?
questions.solution: No real roots ⇔ discriminant < 0 ⇔ k² < 64 ⇔ −8 < k < 8. The integers −7 to 7 make 15 values.

questions.question: If α and β are the roots of x² − 5x + 3 = 0, what is α³ + β³?
questions.solution: α + β = 5 and αβ = 3. α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β) = 125 − 45 = 80.

questions.question: How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy 3x + 5y = 100?
questions.solution: 100 − 5y must be a positive multiple of 3. That needs y ≡ 2 (mod 3) with 5y < 100: y = 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, giving 6 pairs (e.g. y = 2, x = 30; y = 17, x = 5).

questions.question: The digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. Reversing the digits increases the number by 27. What is the number?
questions.solution: Let the number be 10a + b with a + b = 9. Reversing adds 9(b − a) = 27 ⇒ b − a = 3. So a = 3, b = 6, and the number is 36.

questions.question: How many integers x satisfy |x − 3| + |x + 2| < 9?
questions.solution: For −2 ≤ x ≤ 3 the sum is always 5 (6 integers). For x > 3: 2x − 1 < 9 ⇒ x < 5, so x = 4. For x < −2: 1 − 2x < 9 ⇒ x > −4, so x = −3. The answer is x = −3 to 4, which is 8 integers.

questions.question: For which values of x is x² − 7x + 10 < 0?
questions.solution: x² − 7x + 10 = (x − 2)(x − 5) is negative strictly between its roots, so 2 < x < 5.

questions.question: What is the minimum value of (x² + 2x + 9)/(x + 1) for x > −1?
questions.solution: (x² + 2x + 9)/(x + 1) = (x + 1) + 8/(x + 1). By AM–GM this is at least 2√8 = 4√2, with equality when x + 1 = 2√2.

questions.question: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x² − 1. What is the sum of all real x for which f(g(x)) = g(f(x))?
questions.solution: f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1 and g(f(x)) = (2x + 3)² − 1 = 4x² + 12x + 8. Setting them equal gives 2x² + 12x + 7 = 0. The discriminant is 144 − 56 > 0, so both roots are real, and their sum is −12/2 = −6.

questions.question: f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for every non-zero real x. What is f(2)?
What is the minimum value of f(x) = |x − 2| + |x − 5|?
questions.solution: The sum of distances from x to 2 and to 5 is smallest (= 5 − 2 = 3) for any x between 2 and 5.

questions.question: If log₂(log₃(log₂ x)) = 1, what is x?
questions.solution: log₃(log₂ x) = 2 ⇒ log₂ x = 9 ⇒ x = 2⁹ = 512.

questions.question: Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, how many digits does 2⁵⁰ have?
questions.solution: log₁₀ 2⁵⁰ = 50 × 0.3010 = 15.05. The number of digits = ⌊15.05⌋ + 1 = 16.

questions.question: Solve log₂(x − 1) + log₂(x + 1) = 3.
questions.solution: log₂[(x − 1)(x + 1)] = 3 ⇒ x² − 1 = 8 ⇒ x = ±3. But x − 1 > 0 is needed for the log, so only x = 3 works.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 7¹⁰⁰ is divided by 13?
questions.solution: 7¹² ≡ 1 (mod 13) by Fermat's little theorem. 100 = 12 × 8 + 4, so 7¹⁰⁰ ≡ 7⁴ = 2401 = 13 × 184 + 9 ≡ 9.

questions.question: How many divisors of 2⁴ × 3³ × 5² are perfect squares?
questions.solution: A square divisor needs even exponents: 2 ∈ {0, 2, 4} (3 ways), 3 ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways), 5 ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways). 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.

questions.solution: Such numbers are 120k + 3. We need 120k + 3 ≡ 0 (mod 9). 120 ≡ 3, so 3k + 3 ≡ 0 (mod 9) ⇒ k ≡ 2 (mod 3). Smallest k = 2 ⇒ 243.

questions.question: What are the last two digits of 3⁴⁰?
questions.solution: 3²⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 100) (Carmichael's λ(100) = 20; check 3¹⁰ = 59049 ≡ 49 and 49² = 2401 ≡ 01). So 3⁴⁰ ≡ 1 ⇒ last two digits 01.

questions.question: How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 6 but not by 9?
questions.solution: Multiples of 6 in 100–999: 166 − 16 = 150. Those also divisible by 9 are multiples of 18: 55 − 5 = 50. 150 − 50 = 100.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC = 13 cm and BC = 10 cm. What is the inradius?
questions.solution: The height to BC is √(13² − 5²) = 12, so area = 60. s = (13 + 13 + 10)/2 = 18. r = Area/s = 60/18 = 10/3 cm.

questions.question: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm is 6 cm from the centre. What is the length of the chord (in cm)?
questions.solution: Half-chord = √(10² − 6²) = 8, so the chord is 16 cm.

questions.question: From a point P 13 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 5 cm, tangents PA and PB are drawn. What is the area of quadrilateral OAPB?
questions.solution: Tangent length = √(13² − 5²) = 12. OAPB is two right triangles, each (1/2) × 5 × 12 = 30, so the area is 60 cm².

questions.question: What is the area of a regular hexagon with side 6 cm?
questions.solution: A regular hexagon is 6 equilateral triangles: 6 × (√3/4) × 36 = 54√3 cm².

questions.question: A triangle has vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 8). What is the distance between its circumcentre and its incentre?
questions.solution: It's right-angled at the origin, so the circumcentre is the hypotenuse midpoint (3, 4) and R = 5. Inradius r = (6 + 8 − 10)/2 = 2, so the incentre is (2, 2). Distance = √(1² + 2²) = √5. (Check: Euler's OI² = R² − 2Rr = 25 − 20 = 5.)

questions.question: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into solid cones of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are made?
questions.solution: Sphere volume = (4/3)π × 216 = 288π. Cone volume = (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π. 288π/12π = 24 cones.

questions.question: A 12 × 8 × 6 cm cuboid is painted on all faces and cut into 1 cm cubes. How many cubes have no painted face?
questions.solution: The unpainted cubes form the inner block (12 − 2) × (8 − 2) × (6 − 2) = 10 × 6 × 4 = 240.

questions.question: The space diagonal of a cube is 6√3 cm. What is its total surface area?
questions.solution: Diagonal = a√3 ⇒ a = 6. TSA = 6a² = 216 cm².

questions.question: In how many arrangements of the letters of BANANA are the two N's not next to each other?
questions.solution: Total = 6!/(3! 2!) = 60. With the N's together (treat NN as one block): 5!/3! = 20. Not together = 60 − 20 = 40.

questions.question: In how many ways can 10 identical chocolates be distributed among 4 children so that each child gets at least one?
questions.solution: Give each child one first, then share the remaining 6 freely: C(6 + 3, 3) = C(9, 3) = 84. (Equivalently, C(9, 3) by stars and bars.)

questions.question: How many rectangles (including squares) are there on an 8 × 8 chessboard?
questions.solution: Pick 2 of the 9 horizontal lines and 2 of the 9 vertical lines: C(9, 2)² = 36² = 1,296. (204 is the number of squares.)

questions.question: How many four-digit numbers have digits that strictly increase from left to right (e.g. 1357)?
questions.solution: 0 can't appear (it would have to come first). Any 4 distinct digits from 1–9 can be arranged in increasing order in exactly one way: C(9, 4) = 126.

questions.question: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 10?
Two cards are drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are aces or both are kings?
A and B take turns tossing a fair coin, A first. The first to get a head wins. What is the probability that A wins?
What is the sum of all two-digit numbers that leave remainder 2 when divided by 5?
questions.solution: The numbers are 12, 17, …, 97: an AP with 18 terms. Sum = 18 × (12 + 97)/2 = 981.

questions.question: The 5th term of an AP is 17 and the 12th term is 38. What is the 20th term?
An infinite GP has first term 4 and sum 12. What is the sum of its first three terms?
What is the sum of the first 20 terms of the series 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, …?
questions.solution: The terms are triangular numbers k(k + 1)/2. Their sum up to n is n(n + 1)(n + 2)/6 = 20 × 21 × 22/6 = 1,540.

cv-repair.title: Passage: The price of repair
cv-repair.html:
Passage: The price of repair

For most of the twentieth century, a broken household object presented its owner with a simple calculation. A toaster, a radio or a pair of shoes was expensive relative to wages, while the labour needed to mend it was cheap. Repair shops lined the streets of every town, and the decision to fix rather than replace was so obvious that it hardly felt like a decision at all. Over the past few decades that arithmetic has quietly inverted. Manufacturing has become so efficient, and global supply chains so long, that a new appliance can cost less than an hour of a skilled technician's time. The repair shop has not been defeated by consumer laziness; it has been priced out.

Economists recognise this as a version of what is called the 'cost disease'. In sectors where productivity rises quickly, such as manufacturing, prices tend to fall; in sectors where it barely moves, such as hands-on services, wages must still keep pace with the rest of the economy, so prices rise. Repair belongs firmly to the second group. A technician diagnosing a faulty washing machine today works at roughly the same speed as one did fifty years ago, yet must be paid a modern wage. The relative price of fixing things therefore climbs year after year, regardless of anyone's intentions.

This framing matters because it changes what a sensible policy response looks like. If throwing things away were merely a cultural failing, the remedy would be exhortation: campaigns urging people to value what they own. But if the problem is mainly one of relative prices, moral appeals will achieve little. People respond to the costs in front of them, and most households cannot afford to pay more to keep an old machine running than to buy a new one, however virtuous that choice might be.

The more promising interventions therefore target the price gap directly. Some governments have experimented with lowering taxes on repair services, or with requiring manufacturers to sell spare parts and publish repair manuals for a set number of years. These right-to-repair rules are often described as consumer-protection measures, but their deeper effect is economic: by making parts available and designs easier to open, they reduce the hours a technician must spend on each job, and so attack the very cost that made repair uncompetitive.

None of this means that culture is irrelevant. Habits formed when repair was impractical can persist long after the economics improves, and a generation that has never had an object mended may not think to ask. But culture tends to follow prices more readily than it leads them. A society that wants its citizens to repair more would do better to make repair cheaper than to make them feel guilty.

cv-luck.title: Passage: Moral luck
cv-luck.html:
Passage: Moral luck

Imagine two drivers who leave the same party, each having had a glass of wine too many. Both drive home along similar roads with the same degree of carelessness. On the first driver's route, nothing happens. On the second's, a child runs into the street, and the car cannot stop in time. Most of us judge the second driver far more harshly than the first; the law does too, imposing penalties of an entirely different order. Yet the two drivers did exactly the same thing. The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled: whether a child happened to step off the kerb.

Philosophers call this phenomenon moral luck, and the phrase is meant to sound uncomfortable. A widely shared intuition holds that we should be praised or blamed only for what is within our control. The careless drivers controlled how much they drank and whether they chose to drive, but not who crossed their path. If that intuition is right, then the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, and our harsher verdict on the second is a kind of mistake.

The difficulty is that the control principle, applied consistently, threatens to swallow almost everything. We do not control the temperament we are born with, the upbringing that shaped our values, or the circumstances that test them. A person who would have collaborated with a tyrannical regime, had they lived under one, may live a blameless life simply because they were born elsewhere. If we strip away everything that luck has touched, it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged at all.

Some thinkers have responded by biting the bullet: moral assessment, they say, should attach only to the inner will, to intentions and choices, and outcomes are morally irrelevant. This view has the merit of consistency, but it struggles to explain experiences that seem central to moral life. The second driver will rightly feel something the first does not, a particular kind of regret that is more than mere sadness that a bad thing occurred. To tell him that his feelings rest on a confusion seems not merely unkind but false to what has happened.

Others argue that the right response is not to abolish moral luck but to accept it as a feature of our condition. On this view, we are not disembodied wills floating free of the world; we are agents whose actions spill into consequences we cannot fully foresee, and taking responsibility means owning those consequences, including the unlucky ones. The price of this acceptance is that morality becomes less tidy and, in a sense, less fair. But perhaps the demand that morality be perfectly fair was itself a fantasy, born of the hope that we could stand outside the world we act in.

cv-replication.title: Passage: The replication crisis
cv-replication.html:
Passage: The replication crisis

In the early 2010s, researchers in several fields began to confront an awkward possibility: that a substantial share of published findings might not hold up if the studies were simply run again. Large collaborative efforts set out to repeat well-known experiments in psychology, and later in economics and cancer biology, following the original methods as closely as possible. The results were sobering. In several of these projects, fewer than half of the repeated studies produced effects as strong as the originals, and some effects vanished altogether. The episode came to be known as the replication crisis.

It would be easy to read this as a story of fraud, but deliberate fabrication explains only a small part of it. The deeper causes are structural. Journals have long preferred to publish striking, positive results over null findings, and careers depend on publications. Under these pressures, researchers face many small decisions that seem individually harmless: which outliers to exclude, which of several measures to report, when to stop collecting data. Each choice can nudge a result across the conventional threshold of statistical significance. Taken together, such choices can make chance patterns look like real discoveries, even when no one intends to deceive.

The statistical threshold itself has come in for criticism. A result is conventionally called significant if, assuming there were no real effect, data at least as extreme would arise less than five per cent of the time. This is often misread as meaning that there is only a five per cent chance the finding is false. In reality, the probability that a significant result reflects a true effect depends heavily on how plausible the hypothesis was to begin with and on how much statistical power the study had. When many long-shot hypotheses are tested in small samples, a large fraction of the significant results can be false alarms.

Reformers have proposed a range of remedies. One of the most influential is preregistration, in which researchers publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, so that later choices cannot be shaped by the results. Another is the registered report, a format in which a journal agrees to publish a study on the strength of its design, before the results are known, removing the incentive to produce a striking outcome. Larger samples, shared data and routine replication have also gained ground.

Some critics worry that these reforms may stifle exploratory research, the open-ended poking around that often precedes genuine breakthroughs. The reformers' usual reply is that exploration is welcome, provided it is labelled as such. The aim is not to forbid researchers from following hunches, but to stop hunches confirmed after the fact from being presented as predictions made in advance.

cv-translation.title: Passage: Translating poetry
cv-translation.html:
Passage: Translating poetry

There is an old quip that poetry is what gets lost in translation. Like most quips, it contains a truth wrapped in an exaggeration. A poem is not simply a set of statements that could be restated in other words; it is a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations that belong to one language and no other. When a line in Urdu or Tamil depends on a word that means two things at once, or on a rhyme that exists only in that tongue, the translator faces a choice in which something must be given up.

Translators have broadly divided into two camps over how to make that sacrifice. The first holds that fidelity to meaning comes first: the translator's task is to carry across what the poem says, as precisely as possible, even if the result reads stiffly. The second argues that a poem which no longer works as a poem has not been translated at all, only paraphrased. For this camp, the translator must be willing to invent, to substitute a new rhyme or image that produces in the reader something like the effect the original produced in its first audience.

Each position has its characteristic failure. Strict fidelity can yield texts that are accurate in every particular and lifeless as a whole, like a pressed flower that preserves the shape of a bloom but none of its scent. Free recreation, on the other hand, risks replacing the original poet with the translator, so that readers praise a voice that was never really there. Some celebrated translations are admired precisely as poems in their own right, which is both a tribute to the translator and a quiet admission of distance from the source.

A third approach refuses to choose. Some translators publish the original alongside a literal version and a freer rendering, inviting readers to triangulate between them. Others add notes explaining the puns and allusions that could not survive the crossing. These methods ask more of the reader, but they treat the loss honestly rather than disguising it.

Perhaps the most useful way to see the problem is to abandon the idea that a translation could ever be a replacement for the original. A translation is better understood as a reading: one person's careful, partial and inevitably personal account of what a poem is and does. Seen this way, the existence of many competing translations is not a sign that the task has failed, but evidence of the poem's richness. Each version catches a different facet, and no single version, however skilled, can catch them all.
